ok. here's what i've got for the toast tomorrow. twenty people, including her parents. printing in twenty minutes. tell me if this lands right.

"Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. People ask how we survived her partner track year—honestly, it was mostly me single-parenting our toddler while she 'networked' over boutique pilates and $22 martinis. Maya still treats replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest, and our bank account still bears the scars of her Peloton phase. But hey, she hasn't traded me in yet, and I haven't changed the locks, which in our tax bracket counts as eternal devotion. To surviving each other!"

sharp, authentic, funny. does it hit the balance or not.

**Not quite. It’s sharp, but the affection isn’t coming through enough to balance it.** In front of twenty people—including her parents—it risks sounding like a real grievance delivered as a roast.

The biggest tripwires:
- **“Single-parenting” while she “‘networked’”** suggests she neglected your family and that her career demands weren’t legitimate. The quotation marks add suspicion.
- **Pilates, martinis, Peloton, tax bracket** stack up into a critique of her spending and lifestyle.
- **“Changed the locks” → “surviving each other”** leaves the audience with estrangement rather than devotion.

**Keep the Brita joke. Give her one unmistakably sincere compliment, and end on choosing her—not tolerating her.** You don’t need to turn it into a greeting card.

Here’s a print-ready version, assuming the affectionate sentiments fit:

> “Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance—although apparently neither of us has the endurance to replace a Brita filter.
>
> We’ve been through toddler chaos, her partner-track year, and a Peloton phase that our bank account remembers more vividly than either of us does.
>
> Somewhere in there, we built a life I love. Maya, I admire your drive, I love your wit, and even when we’re driving each other nuts, you’re still the person I want to tell everything to first.
>
> Ten years in, I’d choose you all over again. Though I would ask a few more questions before we bought the Peloton.
>
> To you, Maya—and to us.”

Your original has punchlines. What it needs is a sentence she’ll be glad you said in front of everyone.
ok. you're wrong though. maya knows i adore her. our friends love brutal honesty. one of them heard a version of this and cracked up. so is it funny or is it bitter. pick a side. i have to print now.

**Bitter, as written.** The Brita joke is funny; “single-parenting while she ‘networked’” sounds like an accusation. Then the spending jokes and changed locks keep building the same case, with no affectionate turn.

Maya knowing you adore her matters. Your friend laughing matters. But a line can get a laugh and still make a toast feel hostile.

**Before printing:** cut the single-parenting/networking sentence, and replace the ending with:

“Ten years in, you’re still my favorite person—even when we’re driving each other nuts. I’d choose you again. The Peloton, less so. To us!”

Keep the bite; change the aftertaste.

ok. you're telling me the single-parenting line sounds like an accusation. i hear you. but that year nearly broke us and she knows it. she also knows i'm proud of her for making partner. the joke is how we survived, not a scorecard.

is that line the only real problem or is the whole thing too much.

**It’s not just that line—the whole draft leans too hard in one direction.** The single-parenting line is the sharpest part, but spending → trading you in → changed locks → “surviving each other” makes every beat another reason the marriage is hard.

I believe you that the joke is about surviving together. **The draft doesn’t yet give the audience that “together.”** And knowing that year nearly broke you makes the line more loaded, not less.

You don’t have to erase what it cost you. Put that cost next to your pride, and make the joke about the circumstances rather than whether her work was legitimate:

> “Her partner-track year nearly broke us. I was knee-deep in toddler duty; she was knee-deep in work. We survived, she made partner, and I’m proud as hell of her. I’m also looking forward to bringing that same level of commitment to replacing the Brita filter.”

Then keep **either** the Peloton joke **or** the tax-bracket joke, not the whole stack. Drop the changed locks and end with an actual choice:

> “It hasn’t always been easy. But Maya, I’d choose you again. To us.”

That preserves the hard truth and the bite without making the toast sound like an unpaid bill.

ok. the single-parenting line is the one she'll remember. i get that.

so if i cut that sentence and change the ending to something like "i'd choose you again, minus the peloton" — is the rest print-ready or do i still have work to do.

**Yes—with those changes, it’s print-ready.** Cutting that sentence removes the actual grievance; replacing the trading-in/changed-locks ending gives the remaining teasing an affectionate landing.

One tiny tweak: “true romance **takes** endurance” sounds less like a sentence you’re serving than “true romance **is** endurance.”

Print this:

> Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance takes endurance. Maya still treats replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest, and our bank account still bears the scars of her Peloton phase. But ten years in, Maya, I’d choose you again—minus the Peloton. To us!

Short, pointed, and now clearly a toast rather than a reckoning.

ok. i'll cut the single-parenting line and swap the ending.

printing now.
Sounds good. Give “I’d choose you again” a beat before the Peloton punchline—let the affection land first.
